ANNOUNCEMENT OF SIGNING OF AGREEMENT WITH PROVINCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to inform the house of a major milestone in the development of the ARDA program; that is, the signing of agreements between the federal and provincial governments for implementation of the ARDA program in eight provinces, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island, Quebec, Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia. Also, Mr. Speaker, I have just this morning received word that the provinces of Newfoundland and Ontario have signed the general agreement.
These agreements launch the program into action by permitting approval of a wide range of individual projects, and open a broad new held for joint federal-provincial action to develop rural areas and resources. The agreements list nearly forty types of joint projects to permit a broad scale attack on the development problems of Canada's rural areas.
The general agreement provides for a maximum federal contribution of $50 million for programs and projects in all provinces during the initial three year period covered by the agreement. I regard this as a sound investment in economic health and increased productivity in our rural areas. Although these initial agreements are for a three year period only, ARDA is of course designed as a long term program. We are going to use the three years to undertake a large number of pilot projects and extensive research, and to work out the best means of implementing the program's long term goals.
This program has very great import for rural areas, but it has growing importance also for urban dwellers whose need for efficiently produced food and for land for recreational and residential purposes makes their stake in the wise use of the resources of rural areas increasingly great.
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased indeed that the machinery and working policy are now being established through federal-provincial cooperation to get the program into action. I would like to herewith table the general agreement, which is uniform with the provinces, for :he information of members of the house.

1.	Is the government carrying on any research to determine the cause of phocomelia and similar deformities in newborn babies?
2.	Have any government grants been made to any individuals or organizations for the purpose of carrying on medical research into the cause of phocomelia?
3.	How many cases of deformities at birth have been reported to the government in the past year?
4.	How many cases have been attributed to the use of thalidomide during pregnancy?
5.	In cases not directly attributable to the use of thalidomide, has any other cause of deformity been shown?
Answer by: Mr. Monteilh:
1.	The Department of National Health and Welfare in co-operation with the academy of medicine and the pharmaceutical association of Ottawa is conducting a pilot study of the use of thalidomide by pregnant women.
2.	No requests have been received and no government grants have been made directly and specifically for this purpose. Under the national health grants program grants have been given to individuals to support research which may assist in understanding the cause of phocomelia. This includes several projects in the general field of genetics as well as a number of perinatal mortality studies.
3.	There is no routine reporting of birth deformities to the federal government other than those appearing on stillbirth and death certificates. During 1961 the dominion bureau of statistics reported 2,192 deaths of infants and 835 stillbirths attributed to congenital malformations. These deaths and stillbirths are those for which the underlying cause is one of the diseases or conditions specified in the world health organization international

classification, section XIV congenital malformations with respect to deaths, or specified in the classification of causes of stillbirth (Y38), congenital malformations of foetus, in the case of stillbirths.
The provinces have been asked for additional information about congenital anomalies at birth, and some further information should be available later.
In six of the provinces there is provision for reporting congenital abnormalities in live births and stillbirths on a physician's notice of live birth or stillbirth, but there is no regular and uniform tabulation of the data for these provinces. However Ontario, for example, has published data from this source for the years 1959, 1960, as follows:

Answer by: Mr. Green:
The United Nations has not asked Canada for assistance of a purely administrative nature for the United Nations temporary executive authority in West New Guinea, but a request was made for both military and technical assistance in support of the United Nations administration. On August 16, 1962, the acting secretary general asked Canada to provide:
(a) an air adviser of wing commander rank to serve at United Nations security force headquarters;

Canada acceded to the request in full and all personnel and equipment required arrived in West New Guinea on September 2. All costs except regular monthly salaries will be borne by the United Nations, and both personnel and equipment are expected to return to Canada on or shortly after May 1, 1963.

Was radiation leave cancelled or reduced for persons employed as X-Ray technicians in hospitals administered by the Department of Veterans Affairs on or about August of this year and, if so. how many employees were affected by such cancellation or reduction?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: The civil service regulations which became effective April 1, 1962, under the new Civil Service Act do not contain the provision which was included in previous regulations for one week's additional vacation leave for certain employees working in X-ray departments of federal hospitals. However, the regulations provide for leave with pay, with no limitations, to be granted to employees who are found, as a result of regular physical examination, to be in need of such leave because of exposure to radioactivity. It is understood that this is the practice in nonfederal hospitals. The establishment of the Department of Veterans Affairs provides for 87 X-ray operators who may be affected by this regulation.

Agreement between government of Canada and Export-Import Bank of Washington

This agreement made and entered into as of the 12th day of September, 1962 by and between the government of Canada (hereinafter referred to as "Canada") and export-import bank of Washington (hereinafter called "Eximbank"), an agency of the United States of America:
Witnesseth:
Whereas, Canada has applied to Eximbank for a line of credit to assist Canada in maintaining the flow of United States imports: and
Whereas, the granting of such credit will facilitate exports and imports and the exchange of commodities between the United States and Canada:
Now, therefore, the parties hereto agree as follows:
ARTICLE I Line of Credit
Eximbank hereby establishes in favour of Canada a line of credit of four hundred million dollars ($400,000,000) against which Eximbank, acting independently or through the agency of one or more United States commercial banks, will make disbursements, subject to the terms and conditions hereinafter stated, to assist Canada in maintaining the flow of United States imports; it being expressly understood that Canada shall be under no obligation to borrow any specified amount under the line of credit and that disbursements under the line of credit as hereinafter provided shall constitute the borrowings by Canada thereunder,

Availability of the Credit
Two hundred fifty million dollars ($250,000,000) of the line of credit shall be available for disbursement during the period from June 24, 1962 to September 24, 1962 inclusive. One hundred fifty million dollars ($150,000,000) of the line of credit shall be available for disbursement over the period from June 24, 1962 to June 24, 1963 inclusive.

Terms of Repayment and Promissory Notes
Each disbursement under the line of credit shall be evidenced by the negotiable general obligation of Canada in the form of a promissory note. Each such note shall be printed in the English language and shall be substantially in the form of Exhibit A attached hereto and made a part hereof. Each note shall be dated as of the date of issuance.
Questions
shall be payable to the order of Eximbank at such place as Eximbank shall designate and shall be payable both as to principal and interest in lawful money of the United States of America.
The principal amount of each note shall be payable one (1) year from the date thereof. Each note shall bear interest at the rate of four per cent (4%) per annum on outstanding balances, payable semiannually. Interest shall be computed on the basis of actual number of days using a 365-day factor.
Canada shall have the right to prepay, without premium or penalty, at any time or times, all or any part of the principal of a note issued pursuant hereto. Any such prepayment shall be accompanied by interest on the amount of the prepayment accrued to the date of such prepayment.

Disbursements Under the Credit
Subject to the provisions of article VI and IX, disbursements under the line of credit will be made from time to time upon the written request of Canada accompanied by the following:
A.	A promissory note of Canada conforming to the provisions of article III hereof;
B.	Such additional documents and information pertinent to the line of credit as Eximbank may reasonably request.
ARTICLE V Commitment Fee
Canada shall pay to Eximbank a commitment fee computed at the rate of one quarter of one per cent (I of 1%) per annum from June 24, 1962 on the amount of the line of credit as from time to time shall be undisbursed and uncancelled or unexpired. Such commitment fee shall be payable in United States dollars quarterly in advance, the first payment of which shall be due upon execution of this agreement. It is understood and agreed that Canada shall have the right at any time to request cancellation of all or any part of the undisbursed amount of the credit and thereby terminate the commitment fee with respect to any portion of the credit so cancelled and receive a proportionate rebate of the fee theretofor paid.
ARTICLE VI Use of Other Assistance
As a condition precedent to the first disbursement hereunder, Canada shall certify to Eximbank that it has fully utilized the assistance being made available at this time by the international monetary fund and the United States federal reserve banks in connection with Canada's stabilization program.
ARTICLE VII Tax Exemption of Notes
Canada hereby expressly agrees that the promissory notes issued to evidence disbursements under the line of credit, as well as the proceeds and the income of such notes, shall be exempt from taxation or any other charges for any purposes under its laws or any of its political or taxing authorities as long as such notes are held by Eximbank, the government of a sovereign state or a central bank.
ARTICLE VIII Information to be Furnished
A.	Within a reasonable time after each disbursement made under the line of credit, Canada will submit an itemized statement of expenditures, at least equal to the amount of the immediately preceding disbursement, for imports from the United States purchased after June 24. 1962. The itemized

Questions
statement provided for herein shall indicate the general category of the imports; it being understood that, at any time upon the request of Eximbank, Canada shall furnish such additional identifying data with respect to the imports as Eximbank may request.
B.	As long as any of the notes issued under the line of credit shall be outstanding, Canada, at any time and from time to time at the request of Eximbank but not more often than once in any six (6) months' period, will provide Eximbank with such information in relation to Canada's present and prospective balance of payments position and such related aspects of the economy of Canada as Eximbank may reasonably request; it being understood that all such information, if not of public record in Canada, shall be provided in confidence and for the information of Eximbank only.

Legal Opinions and Authorizations
As a condition precedent to the first disbursement under the line of credit, Eximbank shall be furnished the following:
A.	An opinion of the Minister of Justice of Canada, or his deputy, accompanied by necessary documentation, demonstrating to the satisfaction of the general counsel of Eximbank or counsel designated by him, that this agreement as signed on behalf of Canada is legally binding upon Canada in accordance with its terms and that the promissory notes, when and as issued to evidence disbursements under the line of credit, will constitute the valid and binding obligations of Canada in accordance with their terms.
B.	Evidence of the authority of the person or persons who will sign this agreement on behalf of Canada, who will sign the promissory notes and who will act as the representative or representatives of Canada in connection with the operation of the line of credit, together with the authenticated specimen signature, in duplicate, of each such person.

1.	Has the Department of Transport received any report of the ruling of a coroner's jury, held in Toronto last summer and presided over by coroner Dr. Morton Shulman, that the federal Department of Transport approves life jackets which are not safe?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext:
The answers to parts 1, 2 and 3 are as follows: The report referred to has been received but it does not state that the Department of Transport approves life jackets which are not safe although it comments on buoyancy requirements; nor is it the case that there are on the market unsafe life jackets formerly approved by the department.
The primary purpose of a life jacket is to provide buoyancy for the human body and to support the wearer in a safe position when conscious and completely relaxed. It will not automatically turn the wearer on to his back
Questions
in the water or prevent the head of an unconscious person from falling forward and being subject to the action of waves continually splashing on the face, which may result in drowning.
Specifications for Department of Transport life jackets are developed by a committee of the Canadian government specification board. This committee comprises representation from the national research council, the Canadian Red Cross, yachting associations, Y.M.C.A., Boy Scouts Association, harbour police, provincial police, the boating industry, life jacket manufacturers and many others. Life jackets, before receiving approval, undergo exhaustive tests to ensure that they will perform in accordance with specification requirements.
This committee has constantly sought to improve the standards and specifications which are applied but has at no time adopted a standard or specification which is unsafe.

In regard to this question, on October 4 the hon. member for Port Arthur raised a point as to whether it was properly worded. We need not go into what was said on that date, except to say that the conclusion was reached that I would reserve opinion as to the validity of the assertion of the hon. member for Port Arthur, and what might be done to remove a question, which might be found offensive or improper, from the order paper, because at that time I did not feel it was within the power of the Speaker to order that a question either remain on the order paper or be removed from it.
It would appear that the hon. member for Port Arthur raised his question of order on two points, first that part 3 of the question was an assertion of an alleged fact or of opinion, and second, that the assertion might offend the usages, traditions and proprieties of this house.
A quick glance at the notice paper would indicate that many of the questions therein include assertions of fact, stated either implicitly or explicitly. Standing order No. 39, paragraph 1, clearly provides for the use of

Questions
facts in any question. There may be some doubt as to any objections on the grounds of the statement of an alleged fact. However, there then comes the question of opinion, and there is a very fine line of division here. In any event, even if it were opinion and therefore contrary to the orders of this house, I think it is quite readily understood and has been a practice that a question could be redrafted in a minor way, or in a major way if need be, so as to conform; therefore the question need not fall to the ground, necessarily, and be removed from the order paper on that ground.
But to me there is a much more fundamental point involved here. That is the second objection raised by the hon. member, as to whether this question offends the proprieties or the traditions of this house since it deals with a question of the political persuasions, principles or philosophy of a public servant. It would appear that none of the authorities, namely Bourinot, Beauchesne or May, deals specifically with such a question, nor by diligent search by the Speaker or his officers has it been possible to find a definite ruling by any speaker in regard thereto. But I find that in the absence of any known precedent for such a question, and having regard to the principle that a person's political convictions, persuasions or philosophy is a private matter which ordinarily is outside the administrative responsibility of the government or of any governmental corporation or body, and to the further principle that such political convictions, principles, persuasions or philosophy of any public servant is not a question of public concern or of official knowledge unless and until that person participates actively and publicly in a political organization. Therefore it is my opinion that the substance of part 3 of question No. 73 is not in line with the usages and traditions of this house.

If an irregularity should escape the attention of the clerks at the table, the Speaker will point it out before the question is called, and the member is then generally permitted to put the question when he has struck out any objectionable words.
Beauchesne's fourth edition, citation 172, is also applicable but I do not think it is necessary at this stage to read it.
I may also raise this point later this day when certain other questions may come before the house. It is my ruling that paragraph 3 of question 73 should be deleted, and the remainder of the question may be answered as the minister may deem fit.

(Text):
Is the Department of Transport at the present time looking into the possibility of re-establishing, as early as this fall, the night trains between Quebec, Montreal, and Ottawa?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext:
The reply to this question is as follows. The board of transport commissioners advise that the Canadian Pacific Railway Company provided an overnight passenger service between Montreal and Quebec up to May 15, 1961, at which time this service was discontinued. This reduction in passenger train service was investigated by the board and their review of the background leading up to this change indicated that, because of a substantial decline in patronage, the company found it necessary to discontinue the service. It was evident that the patronage of these trains had diminished since the year 1955 by some 45 per cent, and that in consequence of this reduction in passenger traffic the trains were being operated at a substantial loss.
Under the circumstances the board found that the financial improvement for the company in discontinuing the trains outweighed any incidental inconvenience to the travelling public between these points and no action was taken to interfere with the company's proposal. In this connection the board took into consideration the remaining service provided between these two important centres.
The board states that there has been no public demand for a restoration of this service since the trains were discontinued in May 1961, and no action is being taken by the board to have this service restored effective with the fall change of timetable.

WALLACEBURG, ONT.  CLOSING OF SUGAR FACTORY
speechtext:
1.	Is the government aware that the Canada and Dominion Sugar Company factory at Wallaceburg, Ontario, has been permanently closed and will shortly be dismantled?
2.	If so, has the government any plans to assist the sugar beet growers and processors to ensure the preservation of the sugar beet industry in southwestern Ontario and elsewhere?
3.	If the answer is in the affirmative, what steps are being taken in this regard?
Answer by: Mr. Hamilton:
1.	The government is aware that the Dominion Sugar Company factory at Wallaceburg, Ontario, is closed but have no knowledge as to what plans the company may have with respect to this plant.
2.	Sugar beet growers in Canada received no assistance through price support prior to the introduction of the Agricultural Stabilization Act in 1958. Since 1958 sugar beet growers in Canada, including growers in southwestern Ontario, have been assisted by means of deficiency payments. The total assistance provided for the three crop years, 1958 to 1960 inclusive, amounted to $7,042,504.00.
During the past year an intensive review was made of sugar beet production in Canada, following which the method of determining the support level for the 1962 crop was modified. Previously growers had been paid the difference between a prescribed price for beets and returns received by growers from sugar beet processors. On the 1962 crop the amount that the growers will be paid will be determined by the relationship between the value of imported raw sugar and the support level. It is believed this method of providing support should protect the industry from the fluctuations in the world sugar market and thus insure the preservation of the sugar beet industry in Canada.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
In reply to the question raised by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre and the subsequent comment by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillin-gate, may I refer to Hansard of Thursday, February 26,	1959 when Mr. Speaker
Michener, before calling orders of the day, sought to clarify a point on which he had made a ruling on the previous day. I now refer to this ruling. He said:
At the foot of page 1367, the first column, I commented on the procedure in asking that written or starred questions be made orders for returns, and I think I incorrectly stated the effect of the rule- incidentally the rule is No. 39, clause 5-when I said: It is so ordered, then, that this question be made an order for return. Consent of the house is not necessary.
The rule, as hon. members will see, says that the minister having expressed a willingness to lay a return upon the table, his statement shall, unless otherwise ordered by the house, be deemed an order of the house. I did not want the record to be erroneous in the conclusion as to the effect of rule 39.
Another point on the same rule was raised by the hon. member for Laurier, who suggested that a starred question could not be made an order for return under this rule. I find I was correct in rejecting that view. The authority for so doing is the report of the special committee appointed to consider with Mr. Speaker the procedure of the House of Commons. Their report, dated Tuesday, June 14. 1955, which was accepted by the house, states that clause 5 of rule 39 contains a consequential amendment in respect of questions, starred and unstarred, passed as orders for returns. This would clear up that point.

speakeroldname: Hon. George H. Hees (Minister of Trade and Commerce) moved
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-63, to amend the Export Credits Insurance Act.
He said: Mr. Speaker, following discussions which took place last Friday concerning the resolution, we have been able to incorporate in the present bill the very good suggestion made by the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Mcllraith). In order to make it abundantly clear that the maximum liability the corporation may assume under section 14 is limited to $200 million, that is, ten times the paid-up capital and the surplus of the corporation, it is proposed that the word "capital" be inserted before the word "surplus" so that the section will then read:
14. The liability of the corporation under the contracts of insurance issued and outstanding shall not at any time exceed a total of ten times the aggregate of the amount of the subscribed capital and the capital surplus of the corporation.

On Friday we had a good and thorough discussion on the resolution stage. I had intended to make some further remarks at this time, on the opening of the debate on second reading, but looking them over I find they were all dealt with by the questions asked on the resolution stage and the answers I gave then. Therefore, I have nothing more to say at this point, though if hon. members have further questions to ask I shall be glad to try to answer them.

The bill now before us follows the lines discussed during the resolution stage. I believe that over the years the Export Credits Insurance Act has commended itself to members of this house. The Minister of Trade and Commerce was good enough last Friday to give us a comprehensive statement concerning the commodities whose export is being financed under this act-the quantities of certain commodities now covered and the value of certain commodities whose sale is being negotiated at the present time. This particular measure provides for the financing, among other things, of sales of large quantities of wheat to various countries, mainly, though not exclusively, communist countries.
The whole question of Canada's policy with regard to the export of wheat to China, Czechoslovakia, Yugoslavia, Poland and so on has been discussed many times in this house. I would say that in all those discussions the financing of sales of this kind has had the full support of members of the house on both sides. Certainly, one would expect the official opposition to support this measure-as it does-because it is one of those acts which was brought in by a Liberal government and which was used by a Liberal government under the late Mr. C. D. Howe to pioneer in the field of financing credit sales of wheat to iron curtain countries.
This is chamber of minorities. Though we have not been able to detect it in the house to date, nevertheless there have been many statements made outside the house by members of the Social Credit party exceedingly critical of the kind of financing which has been carried out under this measure in connection with the export of wheat. I have in mind a statement issued by the leader of the Social Credit party which was reported on May 22 in the Saskatoon Star-Phoenix:
Selling wheat to China was the most irresponsible act of any government since confederation, national Social Credit leader. Dr. Robert N. Thompson, charged Monday night. "If the wheat was actually filling the empty bellies Mr. Diefenbaker talks about, there might be some excuse, but what consideration has he given to empty bellies in countries as yet uncommitted to communism?"

And so on. The leader of the Social Credit party was very active during the recent election campaign going back and forth across this country criticizing the wheat sales to China. I have in my hand a clipping from the Toronto Telegram of May 18. The heading reads: "Thompson Flays Grain Sales" and the report, datelined Niagara Falls contains this paragraph:
He quoted Lenin as saying that when communism is ready to hang capitalism, the capitalist countries will fight among themselves to see who sells the hanging rope.
I do not know if that rope is supposed to be the wheat but I suppose it is. I have many other newspaper clippings. A headline in the Calgary Herald reads: "Red Sale Hit by S. C. Head"; another in the Saskatoon Star-Phoenix says:	"Selling Wheat to China
claimed Irresponsible". I have in my hand a clipping from the Toronto Star dated June 22, datelined Rouyn, which says:
Twin Social Credit leaders Robert Thompson and Real Caouette joined hands last night to condemn Canada's sale of wheat to red China. Both said they would oppose any move by the federal government to make any more sales.
That seems to make their attitude clear enough. Another article in the Toronto Star of June 23 under a Regina dateline states the following:
Social Credit leader Robert N. Thompson made it clear yesterday his group would balk at wheat or butter sales to communist countries and would attempt to topple the government on this ground.
Well, the Minister of Trade and Commerce made it perfectly clear to us last Friday discussing the resolution that not only had this measure been used in the past in order to help finance sales of wheat to communist countries but that it would be used in the future for the same purpose. I should like to quote from a reply the minister gave as reported on page 456 of Hansard to a question I had asked him; I believe it was I who asked him the question, but it might not have been. In any case, this was the minister's statement:
The hon. member also asked what are the outstanding commitments under section 21 and 21 (a). First of all the commitments under section 21, liability under current policies, are as follows: Yugoslavia. $15.6 million for wheat: Poland, $51 million for wheat . . . United States, $61.8 million for aircraft, making a total of $138.8 million.
Then, Mr. Chairman, our additional outstanding commitments at the present time are $34 million for wheat for Poland; under negotiation or other possible wheat sales amount to $21 million, and for possible aircraft sales to $6 million.
I believe the people of Canada are in favour of sales of this kind-sales of food on credit to nations which have fulfilled the terms of sales which have been made. I am sure that across this nation there is support for sales of this kind whether they be sales
Export Credits Insurance Act of wheat, steel rails or any other commodities which are commodities of peaceful use and cannot be employed in any defence program. I am convinced there is unanimous support for legislation of this kind among grain producers in western Canada of all political parties. I believe that supporters of the Social Credit party, particularly those on the prairies who have wheat to sell, will be very much in favour of the bill which is now before the house, as well as of credit programs of this kind generally. I am pleased to detect what I believe is a complete change of attitude among members of the Social Credit group. I have put on record some of the violent language used in discussing the China wheat sale. I have referred to the stand which has been taken by the leader and deputy leader of that party in regard to the very kind of financing which is provided for under this legislation. The resolution, as far as I can tell, was passed unanimously last Friday. There was not even a voice raised to say: On division. I am encouraged to believe that the members of the Social Credit group are in favour of this legislation now. They have had second thoughts. They have reconsidered their stand and will vote for the bill, just as they voted for the resolution last Friday. Although they have had recent conferences where the whole question has been discussed, they have now reviewed their position-
Reversed it.

Reviewed and reversed it-and are prepared to support legislation which the minister clearly tells us involves the financing of grain sales to various iron curtain countries.
I have in my hand a report from the Toronto Globe and Mail from Langevin Cote, datelined Three Rivers, Quebec, August 27. It states as follows:
The Quebec Social Credit movement yesterday unanimously opposed trade as Canada now carries it on with communist countries, and said it should be limited to barter exchanges without credit.
Of course, this legislation has nothing to do with barter exchanges and it is based on credit; it is based on the principle that the countries which are purchasing our goods live up to their commitments to make certain payments at certain times. It is a credit transaction that as far as I know-the minister can correct me if I am wrong-has been lived up to by the countries purchasing our grain. The prairie grain producers, people who are interested in Canadian trade, in expanding Canadian trade and in promoting exports of Canadian goods will be very interested to see the attitude of the members of the Social Credit party in this house on second

Export Credits Insurance Act reading. Although they have been very critical of this legislation in the past, I hope that their attitude which they took last Friday means they have reversed their stand, and that this legislation may receive the full support of all parties in this house.

Mr. Speaker, one would think from the remarks which have just been made by the hon. member for Assiniboia that this legislation has been brought before us for the purpose only of financing the sale of our exports to communist countries. It has a much broader base than that, unless I am badly mistaken. If the hon. member for Assiniboia would read the copy of Hansard as it records what I said the other day, he would draw very easily my own thoughts in this regard, as I said to the Minister of Trade and Commerce in that I trusted that these credits would be used for the sale of our exports to those countries which are in the immediate area to which we belong and to those which belong to the commonwealth of nations. May I suggest for the benefit of the hon. member for Assiniboia that he knows very well what I said before, but I will say it again so that he understands it without any question. We are not against the sale of our surplus wheat to hungry people who live in countries behind the iron curtain, provided the needs of our friends have been taken care of. That is clear.
What I am concerned about here-and some day the hon. member will look back on what he has said and will think twice about it-is that a moral question is involved which is much deeper than any question of political expediency, or of economic expediency either. The question is whether or not it is advisable for us to be assisting the extension of a way of life that is in bitter contest in the cold war with our own. This is something for every hon. member to think about, because I am convinced that the offensive we face and which stands to threaten our western way of life at this time is an economic one, not military. It is in this regard that we must be very careful about our trade patterns.
What we have said in this house is not a reversal of our stand, because we are practical people, and people must understand that these things are not developed overnight; but also that we must set a principle to follow. In this regard I trust the Minister of Trade and Commerce is making every effort to find markets and to facilitate the sale of our exports to those people who are in equal need with the people behind the iron curtain and who are also hungry, but who are on our side of the fence in this struggle that today reaches right to the very doorstep of this hemisphere.


In this regard I believe that one of the most important things that this house could consider at this time, which I trust the government is doing, is the setting up of a commonwealth trade conference. I know the countries of Africa well. I know the countries of Latin America well. I also know the countries of India and Pakistan, and also of the Middle East. I know that people are starving in those countries today because they have no bread. I trust that the credits which come from a piece of legislation like this will be used to facilitate the sale of wheat to these countries as well.
I also remind my hon. friend from Assiniboia of the fact, that a considerable part of the wheat which we have sold, in the hope that we were reaching the hungry peoples of China, has been used for political purposes. Last Monday I met the new president of the Algerian government at the United Nations, and I was interested to note that only two weeks before, the first shipment of aid to the new country of Algeria there was a gift of Canadian wheat moved into the ports of Algeria in West German boats from China. This is not only true there; it has been true in Korea, in Albania and in other countries. This does not mean to say that the western farmer, or any farmer in Canada, should have his wheat piled up in storage not sold. If the hon. member from Assiniboia would go back and read some of the press clippings he has been talking of now, he would understand, even though he did not belong to the Liberal benches at that time, that the amount of wheat sold in the five years prior to 1957 exceeded the number of bushels of wheat sold in the five years after 1957.
That is not true.

They are statistics. That is one of the reasons that we in the west today- I am a farmer myself-have found that our granaries are empty, as well as our storage facilities, due to the simple fact that during the last two or three years we have not raised the number of bushels of wheat that we did in previous years. This year we thank God for the fact that there is a bumper crop.
Mr. Speaker, when we vote for a piece of legislation like this it is with the hope that some of these credits will be used for the sale of our agricultural produce to those people who live in countries which are friendly to us and which have need of these things. Yes, we support this piece of legislation, not because we have turned our backs on what we said before, but because in principle the thing is sound. We must be able to finance the export of our surplus farm production to those people who are in need of it

to justify our viewpoint. We do not support the legislation for the reasons the hon. member for Assiniboia has tried to put forward, but we do give it support with this word of caution, and again I repeat it. We must do all in our power to make sure that these credits are used for the export of our surplus production, to the end that they might assist those who are friendly towards us. We also remind the Minister of Trade and Commerce of this fact, that what we are doing now is actually using capital which belongs in the realm of tax capital, or is money borrowed by the government for this purpose. I trust it will not be too long before we can have full consideration to the setting up of an export-import bank which will permit us to finance these sales through the facilities of the Bank of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, when this measure was before the house on Friday last in the form of a resolution, speaking on behalf of this party I indicated that we welcomed the measure and considered it as an improvement in the scheme of progress of this corporation. At that time, however, we raised the matter for the consideration of the minister and it is to that matter that I should now like to return. I refer to the failure of the legislation to make provision for extending to underdeveloped countries low interest loans which these underdeveloped countries could then use for purchase of our exports. An examination of the statistics today makes quite clear the need among the underdeveloped nations for loans and credits of this kind. Up to date most of the loans which have been made available to the underdeveloped nations have been made through the world bank for reconstruction and development. During the period of its operations to date it has done a very noteworthy and praiseworthy job. Last year I think it made loans amounting to almost $900 million. As of June 30 of this year, the total amount outstanding was about $6.5 billion. The main trouble with loans made under this agency is that they are made at the going commercial rate of 5 per cent or 6 per cent.
The difficulty that underdeveloped nations of this world are now experiencing is that the amounts of loans for which they have contracted or which they can obtain under the world bank have now reached the point where their export earnings and their economies will no longer permit them to carry any additional loans because of the rate charged and because of the need for the reduction of the principal. A member of the commonwealth, for example, namely India, is indebted to the world bank to the amount
Export Credits Insurance Act of approximately $626 million. India's economy is now reaching the point where she can no longer afford to obtain any further financing of this kind. Hence the need today is for low interest loans to underdeveloped countries.
On Friday I referred the house to a report in the Globe and Mail of that day by Sir William Iliff. In this morning's Globe and Mail there is another report by the same gentleman. In it he is quoted as saying this:
The great need now, he said, is for interest free loans to help the developing countries over the difficult period when debt charges outweigh the improvement in export earnings.
As I have indicated, these underdeveloped countries can no longer afford to obtain financing at commercial rates. In order to meet this difficulty the world bank about a year ago opened up the international development association which provides loans for 50 years at 1 per cent. The situation developing in that institution is that although they had the sum of $760 million available for loans, they are now beginning to see the bottom of the barrel. They have committed over $520 million out of this amount and the funds are expected to be used up by the middle of 1963. What I am trying to emphasize for the consideration of the house is the fact that this problem of obtaining low interest credits is the major difficulty facing the underdeveloped nations.
The annual meeting of the international development association in Washington in September emphasized the extreme urgency for the richer nations, including Canada, to make available these long term credits for the underdeveloped nations. It indicated that it would find no difficulty at all in lending out $600 million each year for at least the next five years, or a total of $3 billion. It is into this great new area of world trade, this limitless market, that we in the New Democratic party would like to see Canada lead the way.
The northern nations of the world are living in comparative luxury while a vast majority of the coloured people are desperately poor. This gap is at present widening. Again, if I may, I should like to refer to the article I quoted earlier by Sir William Iliff. He states as follows:
-living standards in the poor countries have done little more than hold their own since the end of the war.
That is during the last 15 years. Indeed, the problem is becoming accentuated. Since 1947, the population of the world has increased by 700 million. Two thirds of this population increase has occurred in the countries of Asia where the people are already desperately poor and short of food, clothing

Export Credits Insurance Act and shelter. Modern methods of communication have made these people aware of the affluence of the northern countries of the world and they are looking to us for understanding, guidance and assistance. It seems to me that if we fail to meet this challenge they will undoubtedly look elsewhere.
In the past decade it was said that the balance of world power depended upon the recovery of Europe. In the coming decade that same balance of world power will turn upon our rapidly increasing the wealth of the southern peoples. A serious attempt to do this would provide significant export opportunities for Canadian products, particularly processed, manufactured and capital goods. From 1950 to 1958 the southern countries increased their imports by 45 per cent. In 1957 only 70 per cent of this came from the northern countries and amounted to more than $21 billion. Eighty per cent of it was in manufactured goods such as machinery, transportation equipment, chemicals and so forth. The United Nations has estimated that the merchandise imports of the southern peoples from the northern countries during the next 10 years will total $440 billion and will increase at an annual average rate of 5.5 per cent.
It seems to me that these figures open up a staggering opportunity for a country such as Canada with respect to her export trade, if we have the courage and the vision to reach out and accept these opportunities and to take upon ourselves the responsibilities which they impose. These countries are in great need. They cannot get the required capital for further development because they can no longer pay interest and principal charges on any further loans. The only solution now is the provision of low cost loans to these countries whose people are not only hungry for food but hungry for the products that our economy is capable of producing. If we are in a position to extend the necessary credits and loans so that they can buy our goods, they will eventually develop their countries to the point where trade can take place between us.
It seems to me that this is not only a logical attempt at international aid but that it will assist our own export markets. It is in every way in keeping with the tradition that we help each other and that the rich should help the weak.
Previously under the provisions of this legislation when it was introduced in 1944 there was a section under which the government was empowered to make loans to other countries for the purchase of Canadian exports. However, this section was permitted to lapse at the end of 1947 and since that

time it has not been used. As I said earlier, while we welcome this proposal and feel that it is a step in the right direction, we regret that we have not made provision for low cost loans to underdeveloped countries so that they may purchase the products our Canadian economy is capable of producing. It is a step in the right direction, although a timid one. Therefore, I should like to move, seconded by the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond (Mr. Prittie):
That the motion be amended by striking out all the words after the word "that" and by substituting therefor the following words:
"this house declines to proceed with Bill No. C-63 because its terms do not include an extension of the assistance to the governments of other countries provided in section 23 of the Export Credits Insurance Act".
Question.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. The Chair is not satisfied as to form with regard to this amendment and, if hon. members will bear with me, I am seeking advice from the Clerk.

Mr. Speaker, the amendment that has been moved refers to section 23 of the Export Credits Insurance Act. I have a copy of the Export Credits Insurance Act and I cannot see any section 23 as part of that act.
If you will just turn to chapter 105 of the statutes-
What year?
I suspect that the minister is probably examining some pamphlet, but the Revised Statutes of Canada, chapter 105, set out the Export Credits Insurance Act.
What year?
The year is 1952, and there is clearly a section 23.
You are ten years behind the times.
You are the ones who are ten years behind the times.
Mr. Speaker, the Export Credits Insurance Act has been amended in various years since that time. The last amendment was in 1960-61.
March, 1962.

The last amendment, I am advised, was during the last session of parliament in 1962. As far as I am aware, this is the Export Credits Insurance Act as it has been amended from time to time which I now hold in my hand.

On the point of order raised by the minister, I would point out that the section to which my colleague from Danforth has

referred was part of the act as first passed, and as written at that time the section was to expire on December 31, 1947. I assume, therefore, that it was never repealed because it did not have to be repealed, but it was a part of the original act.

It may have been a part of the original act but the parliament of Canada has amended that act on a number of occasions since that time, and what I hold in my hand is the present Export Credits Insurance Act as passed by the parliament of Canada.
Was section 23 ever repealed?

I am not going into the history of the act. All I know is that what I hold in my hand is the present act as it has been passed by parliament and it contains no section 23. Therefore I claim that the amendment is out of order.

Speaking to that point, Mr. Speaker, I should like to point out for your consideration that the original act did contain a section 23 which has never been amended or repealed. The various amendments that were brought into the house from time to time over the years all dealt with sections of the act other than section 23, and it has never been amended or repealed. In my respectful submission it is still valid.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Does the hon. member for Vancouver Centre wish to speak to the point of order?

Yes, Mr. Speaker. Surely when the consolidated statutes came into being in 1952 there was a repeal of any pre-existing statute that was inconsistent therewith. Once consolidation takes effect there is a repeal.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Is the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre speaking to the point of order?

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Speaker. My eyesight is not good enough to see what the Minister of Trade and Commerce has in his hand but I assume it is an office consolidation of the act of the kind on which there is usually a note that it is not something that is used in the courts. May I point out to you, as one or two of my colleagues have indicated, that what this amendment asks is for an extension of something that was provided in section 23 of the act as it was originally passed and as it is on the statute books of Canada in the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1952. If the office consolidation does not contain section 23, that is probably due to the fact that it became inoperative because of the date that appears in section 23, but that goes
Export Credits Insurance Act straight to the point of the amendment, which is that the provision set out in section 23 should now be extended. If it is necessary to add a few words to the amendment to say "as set out in the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1952," that can be done, of course; but surely it is quite clear that what the amendment asks for is the extension of something that is in the original act.
Mr, Speaker, I am advised by the president of the Export Credits Insurance Corporation that section 23, to which hon. members are referring, expired on December 31, 1947.

If the minister will permit me, when we discuss something like this I think we ought to know what section 23 of the act says. It is in these words:
At any time before the 1st day of January, 1948, the governor in council on the recommendation of the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Trade and Commerce may-
Do certain things. It does not provide that he may do those things after the first day of January, 1948. Therefore, since the first day of January, 1948 the things which section 23 of the act provides may be done could no longer be done, but this section is still a part of the statute.
No.

It is there, and all that the amendment says is that the section, which is still in the statute but is inoperative, shall be given effect to again. Surely hon. members can immediately see the difference between something which is deleted and something which becomes inoperative. It is no longer operative but it is still a part of the statute and the amendment says that the section, which is part of the statute but no longer operative, shall now be made operative. With the greatest respect, that is obviously in order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
All I will say to the
house at the moment is that I am still in some doubt as to the relevancy of section 23 which is what really disturbed me in the first place, apart from the fact that this amendment seems to anticipate something that could be offered when we go into committee to give the bill, as a whole, clause by clause consideration. I shall not make a ruling right at the moment but I am grateful to those who have made contributions. I shall give the matter consideration over the dinner hour and announce my decision at eight o'clock.
It being five o'clock this house will now proceed to the consideration of private members' business as listed on today's order paper, namely notices of motions.

subtopic: SUGGESTED EXTENSION OF JURISDICTION TO EASTERN PROVINCES
SUGGESTED EXTENSION OF JURISDICTION TO EASTERN PROVINCES
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this house, consideration should be given to the advisability of extending the jurisdiction of the Canadian wheat board to include the marketing and transportation of wheat for the eastern provinces so as to allow a uniform price inside and outside Canada.
(Translation):
He said: Mr. Speaker, this motion is submitted in the interest of all the farmers in this country. As the western and the eastern farmers both belong to the great Canadian family, it would be illogical that those in the east should have to pay certain commodities $3 more a hundredweight than what the western farmers are receiving. That is why I maintain that we, in the east, will have to talk with the Canadian wheat board, in order to know what interests are interfering, or whether some control is exerted inside that organization, which would result in western farmers getting a sensible price for their grain while we, the eastern fanners, have to pay an exorbitant price, which has led even the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hamilton) to admit that, as a result, 92,000 eastern farms only yield an annual income of $1,200.


If we pay, as I mentioned earlier, an exorbitant price for that wheat it is precisely because we, in the east, never had a chance to make ourselves heard by that board. This is not to say that we would tell the people in the west: "You are getting too much for your wheat." On the contrary, we want them to go on getting that price, but we also want the board at least to enable the eastern farmers not to pay a higher price for Canadian wheat than do the Chinese or the Poles.
If we grant some advantages to those countries, which are behind the iron curtain, why should we not help the eastern farmers in the same way?
Since I have been in the house, I have asked for storage facilities. We are told that in the west this year, there is a surplus of over 500 million bushels of wheat. Well, as the present storage facilities are inadequate, why does the Canadian wheat board not cooperate with the Catholic Farmers' Union or the Federated Co-operative of Quebec who, after all, represent the larger part of the eastern farmers? Why would representatives of those organizations not go and talk over the matter with the members of the Canadian wheat board, and persuade them that the board should immediately have some storage facilities built like those that they have to build in the west. Moreover, they might inform the board of the rail freight tariffs we are quite willing to pay as this is the means of transportation which we are now using. For we

that is the eastern farmers-are of the opinion that if we could do that transport in barges stopping along the deep water wharves which are now found in the east, the freight rate would be considerably lower and consumption of western wheat or grain would rise, because the present cost of the western grain is so high that eastern farmers are no longer interested in producing, and that is why there are those 92,000 farms. Indeed, the people we meet, among them the genial Social Credit members from the west, inform us that the same problems prevail in British Columbia. As a matter of fact, according to the statistics of the Department of Agriculture, there are, in that province, 27,587 farmers, 11,000 of whom earn more than $1,200, but, there too, we find some who earn less than $1,200 a year, which means that 46 per cent of all the farmers in that province are experiencing great difficulties.
If it is now possible to grant, as was suggested during the debate, conditions seemingly favourable for exports, should we not

also think of Canadians, mainly those in the eastern section of the country, who must pay more for their wheat than those countries receiving assistance under the Colombo plan? After the statement made at noon by the minister about the program called ARDA, a program which will revolutionize farming in the province of Quebec, would it not be logical that such credit be used to build warehouses, with the agreement of the Canadian wheat board?
A fair solution is now sought to our farmers' problems; well, the government should not think only of the western farmers but also of their eastern counterparts.
I suggest that after a national survey, we would be in a position to increase productivity on the farms of our section of the country with the assistance of the Canadian wheat board provided representatives of the Quebec federation of co-operatives and the Catholic Farmers' Union sat on that body.
The support price of 34 cents for eggs announced by the Minister of Agriculture for this year is barely sufficient to prevent the farmers from starving to death, since it equals the cost of the grain we have to purchase at a price which is much too high at this time.
This is why, in my estimation, we could obtain feed grains at a much reduced price if the moneys paid in contribution to the Colombo plan were used to assist the eastern farmers; it would also be more advantageous, as I said, than to sell such grain to the Chinese and the Russians at a lower price than that paid by the eastern farmers. If we built warehouses along the wonderful St. Lawrence river, from Fort William, that grain could be shipped around the Gaspe peninsula and even into lake St. John area, and the number of buyers in the province of Quebec would thus be considerably increased.
Since the Catholic Farmers' Union represents 38,000 farmers, it would be normal for the Canadian wheat board to look after the farmers the same way a family looks after its members and to offer the eastern farmers advantages as interesting as those offered at the present time to foreigners by western Canada.
In the province of Quebec, we want to live on our family farms. But when we have to pay higher interests, not to speak of unreasonable profits, the prices become excessive. As we buy 75 per cent of the basic grain production, I say that there should be no control and that individuals should not be permitted to take unfair advantage of us.

Although western farmers do not seem to be satisfied with the prices they are receiving, eastern farmers, as I mentioned earlier, have to pay up to $3 more per hundred pounds for the grain they have to buy.
There lies the real fault in this illogical situation, and if speedy action is not taken within a few years, some 10,000 to 12,000 family farms will be closed down, and their people will trek to the cities where they will swell the ranks of the unemployed.
If I have failed to convince the Minister of Agriculture of the necessity to build warehouses immediately, before navigation stops on the St. Lawrence river on December 15, in order that they may benefit the people this very winter, then 5,000 farms will have to be abandoned and those people will be starving this winter.
As it is necessary to feed mankind today, we, the eastern farmers, are willing to go on producing, on condition that we shall be looked after, because we are not any greater dolts than other farmers in this country.
In Quebec, we intend to produce, we intend to grow crops, if we are paid sensible prices for our grain and not exorbitant ones, because of a too high interest rate, as the people in the west are ready to sell us their grain. There are 2 billion human beings who are starving and we, Catholics of the province of Quebec, do not intend to just sit there, for we want to produce; at present, the situation is illogical. That is quite inconsistent. Those conditions must stop, and quickly too, because our farmers are getting impatient.
On June 18 last, 26 members from Quebec asked for those things; they were, indeed, quite satisfied, in their minds, that it was time to ask for the eastern farmers' due.
Earlier today, I saw our socialist friends opposite rise with the standing orders in their hand. Laws are all right. They are necessary. But, if we do not legislate in regard to the needs of people who are now in a difficult position, our friends the socialists will only give further help to the communists.
Anyway-and I have heard it frequently- we are told many things about planning in agriculture. There is no question of planning. All we want is to be sold grain cheaper, so as to be able to produce at a profitable price in our part of the country. For, according to Khruschev's own statements, planning in Russia and China seems to have been a tremendous failure. The land cannot be managed at will.
Since this grain has been produced by the western farmers, we wish to have our share of it and to have it at a reasonable price, for the government's policy of a minimum price

We would then stop asking for subsidies. It is not subsidies we want, but favourable prices, since we are living in Canada.
A French author once wrote that our country consisted of 30 acres of snow. But just the same, we want to live in Canada, we love our country and shall remain here. Of course, we shall never be able to compete with certain countries, Australia, for instance, which can produce butter at 22 cents a pound.

Mr. Speaker, before I deal with this matter this afternoon I should first of all like to congratulate you on your elevation to your high office. This is the first opportunity I have had. I do so on behalf of the people of my riding, many of whom came from the province of Quebec and also from France, and who are interested in the fact that you represent both the historic races in Canada.
The resolution before us moved by the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Dumont) is as follows:
That, in the opinion of this house, consideration should be given to the advisability of extending the jurisdiction of the Canadian wheat board to include the marketing and transportation of wheat for the eastern provinces as well as for the western provinces so as to allow a uniform price inside and outside of Canada.
The first thing that occurs to me is that possibly we should go back to the beginning when the Canadian grain board was first brought into the House of Commons back in 1935 and to the debates of June 10 when the prime minister of that day, namely the Right Hon. R. B. Bennett, moved the following resolution as found at page 3456 of Hansard of that year:
That it is expedient to bring in a measure to establish a board to be known as the Canadian grain board with power to purchase, receive and take delivery of wheat, oats, barley, rye and flax seed, or any one or more of such grains for marketing and to sell, store, transport and market such grains, and to provide for the appointment of such clerks, employees and assistance as may be necessary-
And so on. At that time in the House of Commons when this measure was brought in I believe it is fair to say there was considerable opposition from the members of that party now forming the official opposition in the house. They were opposed particularly to the compulsory features of the Canadian Wheat Board Act. Before I go into that particular part of the matter I might quote from Mr. Bennett who, speaking in debate on June 12, 1935, had this to say as found at page 3577 of Hansard of that year:
The terms and provisions of the bill are short and simple. It provides for the marketing of the Canadian wheat crop through the channel I have indicated, not through a private enterprise. It is to be
542	HOUSE OF
Extension of Jurisdiction of Wheat Board done through a public board created by the dominion of Canada for the purpose of ensuring against the destruction of that measure of economic stability, weak though it may be, that we through our efforts have been able to build up in the last few years.
He made that statement because of the situation which had prevailed in Canada in 1929 and 1930 when we saw the surplus of wheat in this country rise as it had never risen in any period prior to that time. I need not remind hon. members of this house that the government of that time was led by Right Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King.
A few moments ago I said that the opposition to the wheat board act at that time was directed against the compulsory features. I will refer to the speech of J. L. Ralston on June 13, 1935, in which as found at page 3597 of Hansard of that year, he said this:
I would strike out or eliminate the compulsory feature which is contained in this bill. Mr. McFarland has no compulsory power to make people sell their wheat to him, but this act by virtue of giving control over the elevators does create a situation whereby the whole grain trade is tied up and made subservient to this board.
That has remained essentially the purport of the act up until this time. When I look at this resolution I just wonder whether the hon. member really meant he wished consideration to be given to including the marketing of grain or wheat in eastern Canada and central Canada and having it marketed in the same way as it is marketed in western Canada today under the Canadian wheat board. In fact, as I think back over the last four or five years of those things that have come to our desks as members of parliament from the wheat producers of Ontario and the grain producers in eastern Canada generally, it would seem to me that they have not been asking that the Canadian wheat board take control of the marketing of their products here in eastern Canada.
The other thing that I was wondering about is why the transportation of wheat is mentioned. I would have thought that the feeders and the livestock producers in central Canada and eastern Canada might be more concerned with oats and barley than with wheat alone. However, I just draw that matter to the attention of the house for the consideration of hon. members at this particular time.
All of us are naturally in favour of building up a sound agriculture policy in Canada. We realize that this entails a general feeding policy in Canada and the development of the livestock industry in many areas of Canada where today there are lands which are practically lying idle and which could be used to advantage in that regard. However, when an hon. member


representing his party rises in his place in the House of Commons and indicates that they would like to strike off approximately $1 per hundredweight from the grain that has come from western Canada, I think it opens up a whole wide question for all of us to take a good look at. I think that question could very well be asked by some of those who produce grain very close to where the hon. member lives. If we are going to strike off $1 per hundredweight from grain from western Canada, what are we going to do about the grain that is produced in Ontario, in the province of Quebec and in the maritimes?
With regard to representation on the Canadian wheat board, may I say it is a known fact that there is an advisory committee from eastern Canada. This committee is composed of six members:	two from
Ontario, two from Quebec and two from the maritime provinces. I believe they will be meeting in the very near future. I know that all of us in the house have looked forward to the constitution of this committee, in the hope that they will be able to give some worth-while advice to the board at such time.
The matter of elevators in central and eastern Canada is not a new one. It has been raised many times in the past by advocates from various parties. We in western Canada particularly have thought that storage elevators in the eastern part of the country and in central Canada as well might be of great benefit to us. We have often wondered why the co-operatives in those areas of the country have not made more use of their co-operative strength in the purchasing of grain. Those hon. members who are familiar with what the co-operatives have been able to do in western Canada will know that here is a field in which there is room for a great deal of activity. Often a co-operative can do something on behalf of its members much better than can a government and, incidentally, at less cost as well.
I should like to put this on the record. Mention was made of $3 per hundredweight for wheat, with an initial payment of $1.23. You have a final payment and subsequent payments which were about 39 cents, I believe. You get about $1.62. That is for 60 pounds of wheat. If you take 100 pounds you have $3. You also must take into consideration handling charges and those things have to be paid by the person who is producing just in the same way as with our grain going into the export market.
I would be interested in hearing the other front bench members of the Social Credit party let us know what they think of this

bill. After all, this is a very interesting situation. It is one in which we are all interested. I am interested in the hope expressed by the hon. member for Bellechasse that they can knock $1 off a hundredweight of wheat from western Canada. We in western Canada have felt that we have not been securing what you would call a fair enough price for grain throughout the years. If you had been here during the last several years you would have experienced some of that play here in the House of Commons and across the country whereby the grain producers in western Canada were asking for substantial subsidies.

The unwinding of the wheat marketing problem in the future is going to require not only the patience, courage and understanding of all concerned, whatever their personal views, but also a willingness on the part of the Canadian taxpayer to accept, if necessary, any temporary financial burden that may arise. We worked very closely with them and we in western Ontario feel that right across the province corn could be grown as far north as No. 7 highway in view of the modern breeding of hybrid corn. We would have no trouble at all proving we could grow the corn if we were given a fair return for our efforts.
On my own farm I had 100 acres of corn this year which we are now harvesting. We in western Ontario have had one of the biggest yielding crops of corn we have had in a good many years. I am sure that the government can take no credit for that. Maybe they will try to, but the credit belongs to God and the farmers. We had extraordinarily good growing conditions in that area which resulted in one of the best crops in years. In years to come we can produce corn as a high energy feed grain that will take the place of a lot of the other grains and it will produce quality beef, pork and turkeys. We have shipped this grain to the maritimes before through our own local co-operative. We know we can ship corn to that area. I believe that the first corn to go into the maritime provinces went from southern Ontario and it was the high protein, high quality grain that the people there like. It was our own farm organization that asked that subsidy be paid on feed grain going into the maritime provinces, but to our amazement the subsidy was paid on United States grain entering that area. We did not think that was fair and we do not think so now.

speakeroldname: Hon. George H. Hees (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the
Export Credits Insurance Act was passed in August 1944 it was in three parts. Part I is the responsibility of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, and this part established the Export Credits Insurance Corporation. The legislation before the house, Bill No. C-63, refers only to part I.
Part II authorized the government to make loans to devastated countries, and was the responsibility of the Minister of Finance. The right to make loans under part II expired on December 31, 1947.
The amendment moved by the hon. member for Danforth (Mr. Scott) is, I submit, out of order because the resolution which it seeks to amend was approved by the house last Friday.
Briefly, the bill deals with part I of the act. The sections which the bill seeks to amend are contained in part I of the act and deal with the operations of the corporation, the purpose of which is to assist Canadian producers to sell more goods in all parts of the world. What the hon. member wishes to do is have the government provide long term loans to developing countries. This is one of the purposes of section 21(a) as it operates at the present time and as it will operate more efficiently when the present bill is passed.
Section 21(a) provides $300 million-I repeat $300 million-for that exact purpose. Already contracts under section 21(a) amounting to more than $50 million have been signed during the past year, and commitments have been given for additional business totalling $75 million, all in developing countries.
As an example of the type of loans being made under section 21(a) I can mention the $25 million credit-
