With respect to the serious point the minister raised in opening his remarks after eight o'clock, I must say he raised a point that has to be considered by anyone seeking to move an amendment of this kind. That point is clearly this: is the proposed amendment covered within the framework of the resolution that the house passed on which the amending bill is based?
I draw your attention, sir, to the terms of the resolution which this house passed. It reads as follows:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Export Credits Insurance Act to increase from two hundred million dollars to four hundred million dollars the limit of the liability of the Export Credits Insurance Corporation under contracts of insurance entered into under section 21 of the act;
At that point there is a semicolon, and the rest of the resolution reads:
and to provide further for certain changes in connection with the administration of the act.
Export Credits Insurance Act
Now, Mr. Speaker, the only thing that is referred to precisely in the resolution is the increase from $200 million to $400 million, to which I have already referred, and that is carried out in clause 2 of Bill C-63 that is now before us. But the same bill, C-63, has in it clauses 1 and 3 which propose to do things which were not specifically referred to in the resolution. They are, I take it, covered by that general phrase "and to provide further for certain changes in connection with the administration of the act".
This is another case, Mr. Speaker, of a widely, generously worded resolution. We have had many of them through the years. When my hon. friends across the way sat on this side of the chamber, they did it a number times. It is a well established rule that when the resolution is so broad that it covers a multitude of things that can be done, then it is open to hon. members of the house to move amendments that are within that framework.
I suggest that if propositions such as are contained in clauses 1 and 3 of the amending bill, which were not specifically named in the resolution, are in order, it is in order to bring in other proposals which can be classified as changes in connection with the administration of the act. That is precisely what my colleague's amendment seeks to do; it seeks to make a change in connection with the administration of the act.
In his opening remarks at eight o'clock tonight the minister said that the bill he has brought in deals only with part I of the Export Credits Insurance Act. But the resolution did not confine the proposed amendments to part I of that act; it was broad enough to cover any changes in connection with the administration of the act. The reference there is to the whole act.
I submit therefore, Mr. Speaker, that the proposal contained in the amendment moved by my colleague is relevant to the bill, which seeks to amend the Exports Credits Insurance Act, and that in so far as it is an administrative change, it has been covered by the resolution which the house passed on Friday last.
While I am on my feet may I say, Mr. Speaker, that before an amendment of this character is moved from this corner, some research into what has happened in the past has always been carried out. This particular type of amendment, an amendment to second reading of a bill, is one in connection with which there is a long list of precedents. I draw your attention tonight only to one. It is found on pages 426, 427 and 428 of the Journals for 1959. The ruling given there is by Mr. Speaker Michener. It was on a second reading amendment, moved by the hon. member for Essex

Export Credits Insurance Act East (Mr. Martin), to a bill amending the Unemployment Insurance Act, which read:
This house declines to proceed with a bill, the terms ot which do not provide-
Such and such. I need not give the whole of it. The point of drawing attention to this ruling is that it was a case where the right of the hon. member to introduce such an amendment was contested. It was considered seriously; it was considered overnight, and Mr. Speaker Michener ruled, in line with what I have just said regarding this proposed amendment, that it was correct in form and it was covered so far as its provisions were concerned by the general nature of the resolution that had preceded the bill brought in by the government.
As I say, Mr. Speaker, there are many instances, but this is the most recent one I have been able to find concerning which a point of order was raised. The point of order having been raised, the matter having been considered thoroughly by Mr. Speaker Michener, he concluded his remarks by saying:
As I say, it appears to me to meet the precedents and the rules of the house and therefore I am prepared to allow the amendment.
I suggest that the amendment my colleague has now moved is on all fours with the amendment that was moved on May 12, 1959, which was allowed on that occasion by Mr. Speaker Michener, and this amendment should likewise be allowed.

Mr. Speaker, may I say a word on the point of order which has been raised, dealing principally with the objection that has been suggested which is based on the allegation that section 23 is no longer in force. Section 23 provides that at any time before January 1, 1948 the governor in council may, if he deems it advisable, do certain things. If the amendment were one, or if there were a motion before Your Honour which simply provided for the deletion of the words "before January 1, 1948" from the legislation, there would be no question whatever that the legislation would be still in force. In fact, Your Honour, I suggest that this house, when it passed the Interpretation Act, realized there was a vast difference between the provisions of a statute which might be repealed and the provisions of a statute which might for one reason or another cease to have effect, because in section 11 of the Interpretation Act parliament dealt with the question of the operation of statutes, and in section 19 of the Interpretation Act parliament dealt with the repeal of statutes.
The minister might argue that this particular provision in section 23 has become

obsolete, but it is a well established principle that a law is not repealed by becoming obsolete. I cite as authority for that proposition the tenth edition of Maxwell on the Interpretation of Statutes. Maxwell in that well known work points out that trial by battle, which was established under a statute of Henry II in the twelfth century, had become obsolete by 1819, and yet it was deemed by the courts at that time to be still in force.
I am not suggesting that the legislation passed by the previous government in the immediate post-war years, or any of it, is as obsolete as trial by battle; but I do suggest that the principle is still the same and ought to be applied in this case; that section 23 is still in force and cannot be regarded as having been wiped from the statute books, and can be subjected to such an amendment as the hon. member for Danforth (Mr. Scott) has moved.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member seems to be worried by what he believes to be the inability of the government under this present act to make loans to other governments. That is not the case. I wish to thank hon. members for having advanced arguments in this connection. First of all, in order to dispose of the argument raised by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre in citing a ruling by His Honour Speaker Michener on May 12, 1959, I would draw to the hon. member's attention a certain distinction which the Speaker at that time indicated was very germane to the nature of the amendment then before him.
I read from page 427 of the Journals- the second last paragraph on the page. The first sentence reads:	"It is a resolution
declaratory of a principle adverse to the main principle of the bill". This is not applicable

Export Credits Insurance Act in my estimation in this instance. That would therefore dispose of the precedent as not being applicable.
Considering this question generally, it is competent for a member on second reading of a bill who desires to place on record any special reasons for not agreeing to the second reading of a bill to move as an amendment to the question a resolution declaratory of some principle adverse to, or differing from the principles, policy or provisions of the bill, or expressing opinions as to any circumstances connected with its introduction or prosecution or otherwise opposed to its progress. I suggest that this amendment is not one adverse to a principle of the bill, but is one otherwise opposed to its progress or seeking information on its progress. Those words are generally contained in Beauchesne's fourth edition citation 382. I would point out to hon. members that it is a fundamental principle that no matter ought to be raised in a debate on a question which would be irrelevant if moved as an amendment, and that an amendment cannot be used for importing arguments which would be irrelevant to the main question. In this regard I would refer hon. member's to May's sixteenth edition at page 421. Again, citing May at page 531, I quote:
The principle of relevancy in an amendment governs every such motion. The amendment must "strictly relate to the bill which the house, by its order, has resolved upon considering".
The proposed amendment clearly states that it has reference to section 23 of the main act. No provision can be found in the bill before the house which is related to that clause. Accordingly, if the provisions of section 23 of the act can be brought before the house by virtue of an amendment, I would submit that other sections of the main act could also be brought forward in the same fashion. Therefore, I would submit that the amendment does not oppose any principle or provision of the bill; in other words, the subject matter of the proposal is a substantive motion and an entirely new question unrelated to the bill before us. In the present instance I do not consider this amendment relevant to the bill being discussed; it is rather relevant to the act itself. But at the moment I respectfully submit that we are not discussing the act; we are discussing Bill No. C-63.
It is my opinion that the rule of relevancy is completely disregarded. If every bill that was discussed by this house was subject to amendments of this type which could stipulate that the bill did not contain enough and should contain something else, then there would be no relevancy at all.
In this connection I would refer hon. members to a ruling by Mr. Speaker Macdonald,

reported at page 237 of the Journals under the date of November 14, 1949. He said:
On the second reading of an amending bill . .. it is the principle of the amending bill, and not the principle of the act to be amended, which is the "business under consideration". The discussion must therefore relate exclusively to the principle of the amending bill.
May I add that here, where we are referring to "discussion", we also include "amendments", which must relate exclusively to the principle of the amending bill.
In addition, if I may cite a ruling of Mr. Speaker Michener on December 13, 1957 while the house was considering a motion for the second reading of Bill No. 232 to amend the Income Tax Act, the then Speaker, as reported at page 2313 of Hansard, said:
This is an act to amend the Income Tax Act and it is relevant, as I understand the precedents, to discuss the sections of the Income Tax Act which are to be amended by this bill but not to review the act as a whole.
With the greatest respect to the mover and seconder of this amendment, I am of the opinion that that would be the purpose of their amendment and that it is irrelevant, and I so rule.

I feel very strongly that nothing should be left undone to continue our efforts to promote our exports, and I welcome the increase in funds from $200 million to $400 million which is to be made available to Exports Credits Insurance Corporation. The success of the operations of the corporation is best illustrated by the fact that over $1 billion of export sales have been insured since the first policy was issued by the corporation. During that time the corporation has been able to make a modest profit on transactions and has operated at no expense to the Canadian taxpayers.
Mr. Speaker, three years ago I had the privilege of sponsoring in this house a bill of incorporation setting up the Exports Finance Corporation. This was the first company in Canada to enter the export finance business. The charter of this company has recently been acquired by the chartered banks of Canada and is working closely with the Export Credits Insurance Corporation in promoting the sales of our goods and services abroad on a credit basis.

To a great extent we in Canada have overcome the problems of production, and I know that this is particularly true of agriculture. But it is in the area of distribution that much remains to be done. I think this government has faced up to this problem and that both industry and agriculture have benefited under the capable salesmanship of the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the Minister of Agriculture, both of whom have been inspired by the able leadership of our Prime Minister.
Recent sales of wheat have been encouraging. However, when one considers the levies imposed on our wheat by the European common market countries and the implications posed by the entry of our best wheat customer into that market, there is every reason to believe that Canada's grain business will suffer immeasurably unless we are able to find additional markets. I should like to point out to hon. members that while our wheat enters Britain free of duty, the levies imposed by the E.C.M. countries, according to the latest figures, are: Germany $1.94 a bushel; France $1.11 a bushel; the Netherlands $1.15 a bushel; Belgium $1.12 a bushel; and Italy $1.47 a bushel. Mr. Speaker, when the resolution was before the committee I expressed concern over a question of principle involved in this new bill. I stated then-I might say that I have not talked with any hon. members who differ from this opinion and I have spoken with a number of them-that I did not see how there could be any opposition to the principle of the raising of the limit or the ceiling of credits which the Export Credits Insurance Corporation might extend in order to expand exports. But I was concerned and I still am concerned about the fact that I now find that this corporation, which was set up in 1944 to insure against foreign exchange risks and other matters of that sort, is going into the commercial banking field. The first move was made in 1959 when the limit was raised to $200 million, and loans in this major field were then predicated upon the approval or authorization of the governor in council. When authorized by the governor in council the corporation may guarantee, may lend money and may do these other things.
In the bill before us it is proposed that the governor in council jointly with the Export Credits Insurance Corporation will go one step further. The corporation will now be able to take notes in their own name from the importer in the foreign country. The Canadian exporter will be completely bypassed. Furthermore, it is proposed that the corporation can turn around and sell or discount the paper they have taken in their own name without the Canadian exporter coming into the picture at all. That is a most extraordinary situation if we study it, and my concern is not that we are going to expand credit from $200 million to $400 million but that we are going to put an insurance corporation into the commercial banking field. What is more, it is a field of banking where the government comes into the picture and where political pressures or influences may come into the picture. That is as clear as it can be. It is only when authorized by the governor in council that these moves can be made. It is not the bank that is instituting these things; it is the government.
Take the situation at the present time, for example. Loans totalling nearly $200 million have been made or committed and, according to the figures given by the Minister of Trade and Commerce yesterday, $107 million of that amount is for wheat sales alone and wheat sales to communist countries. I am not opposed to the sale of wheat to communist countries or to anyone else if they need food, 27507-3-36i
Export Credits Insurance Act but $107 million of this amount is for the sale of wheat alone under the theory that this is a loan to expand our exports to these countries. We are expanding one class of exports only, primarily wheat.
It does seem to me that it would be much more sensible if this additional credit facility were left in the hands of a banking institution. We do not necessarily have to create an export-import bank such as they have in the United States but surely by an extension of the provisions of the Industrial Development Bank Act we could cover a situation of this kind and remove it from the field of politics or political pressure completely. It is a matter of serious concern, Mr. Speaker, that we should find the government going into commercial banking when there is the possibility of political influence in the background.

Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that, as on the resolution stage of this measure, we have got into a detailed debate on something concerning which I think all parties are in general agreement in that they are in favour of the legislation. I think we are wasting time and the question should be called.

Mr. Speaker, I want to be very brief in this matter and initially I wish to associate myself with the remarks of the hon. member for Assiniboia and other members on this side of the house expressing approval in principle of the bill and the expansion of credit to facilitate exports from Canada. I do not want to repeat the various commodities to which other members have referred in supporting the bill but I want to say this to the Minister of Trade and Commerce. I respectfully direct his attention to consideration of the use of the expanded credit facilities to bring about a larger market abroad for tobacco grown in Canada. In saying this I want to compliment the minister in general for what I personally conceive to have been a good job done by him during his term of office.
In my riding of Durham and in other areas of central and southern Ontario as well as elsewhere in Canada the growing of tobacco is an important industry. It is an industry that can facilitate our economy generally particularly if export markets for tobacco can be located and developed. If we can locate and develop export markets we will have a tremendous opportunity to throw away the existing bonds of acreage control which now govern farmers engaged in the production of tobacco and thus expand this industry substantially in Ontario and other parts of Canada. I say that this is one very useful industry in which this additional

Export Credits Insurance Act credit could be employed and I commend this thought to the minister for his consideration.

Mr. Speaker, as this is the first time I have had the opportunity of rising with you in the chair may I add my felicitations and congratulations on your election to the numerous ones already extended to you by other hon. members. I have already spoken on the resolution stage of the bill and my remarks now will be very brief, I hope.
With respect to my remarks on the resolution I indicated at that time, as have a number of other speakers, approval of the method in which the business of the corporation has been conducted since its inception. I repeat that, and my suggestion tonight is rather a logical conclusion to this summation. The minister in introducing the bill said that it had two main purposes. One was to increase the authorization and scope of the business of the corporation. The second was the elimination of unnecessary red tape and government formalities. In respect of the latter I might suggest we look in particular at the financial-if one may call it that

history of the corporation.
The work of the corporation, or its functions, may be divided into roughly three categories. One is that of insurance to which the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Nicholson) referred. In respect of the insurance function the act originally provided that the insurance business would be conducted entirely by the officers of the corporation and the board of directors. Subsequently when the business of the corporation was to be expanded, an additional provision was made whereby for business which was assumed to be outside the normal course of the operation of the corporation, namely in respect of special commodities or in respect of some sums which were in themselves, or singly very large, and in respect of countries to which the proportion of credit seemed to be unduly high, then additional business could be conducted solely upon authorization of the governor in council; and while the powers of the corporation to transact business on its own was limited to the sum of $100 million, an equal sum was provided for the transaction of business under authorization of the governor in council.
Subsequently there has been an increase in the authorized subscribed capital of the corporation with the result that the corporation can now transact business on its own in the amount of $200 million as against the original $100 million, and the amount of

business subject to the authorization of the governor in council has been raised to $200 million.
The proposal in the bill tonight is to raise the ceiling, for the type of business which requires the authorization of the governor in council, from $200 million to $400 million.
I would suggest to the minister that in view of the excellent record of the corporation, and having in mind that the business of the corporation appears to have expanded very substantially right across the entire spectrum of the kind of business it does, it would be more appropriate, and would cut out a considerable measure of the government red tape for which the minister rightly has some disdain, if instead of increasing the authorization under which business can be done with the authority of the governor in council the authorization could be increased under which the corporation can do business in its own name.
Unfortunately I have not a specific amendment to suggest but would merely like to commend this to the attention of the minister.

Mr. Speaker, I feel that the majority of the hon. members of this house agree upon the principle of the bill.
We are particularly interested in two aspects of the measure, the financial aspect and the social aspect.
If, for example, this legislation is such that it will open to us the doors of South America especially, then it becomes hard to reject, because it must be realized that South America is made up of countries with which we have much in common on the spiritual plane and to which we must give special assistance.
Therefore, this legislation must enable us to have our doors wide open for South American countries. That is why, as regards the principle of the bill, I think we agree.
However, the financial side of the legislation must also be taken into account. I do not think it wise that the funds required to increase the social capital provided for under the legislation should be drawn from the tax capital. We must use the funds available at the Bank of Canada, because it is the country's bank, and its funds must be used especially to increase the social capital of the Export Credits Insurance Corporation.
Those are, Mr. Speaker, the two points I wanted to raise concerning this bill, its financial aspect and its social aspect.

Mr. Speaker, the resolution stage provided for a bill to double the amount of insurance available under section 21 of the act and to provide further for certain changes in connection with its administration. I suppose this is a minor point, but under section 14 of Bill C-63 there is a provision for a change in the liability of the corporation. We did not have notice of that and I am glad to have an opportunity to talk about section 14 as otherwise I would be out of order.
When speaking the other day on the resolution stage the minister said we should go back to our constituencies and call to the attention of small exporters that the facilities provided by the act would be freely available to them. I believe this should be done but I have found that the small occasional exporter, such as the man who might sell three, four or five carloads of pulpwood or two or three carloads of processed pulp to the United States, is not aware that he can qualify under section 14 of the act.
I also found that there is some confusion in the wording of the act. For instance the word "exporter" has three or four definitions. "Exporter" as it applies to section 14 and to most of the act is defined as one who exports or agrees to export goods from Canada. In section 13 this definition is enlarged to include Her Majesty in right of Canada.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. I am wondering
whether the hon. member is going to produce any argument in this regard because it seems to me he is embarking on consideration of various sections of the act and not on consideration of the bill. At this stage we are discussing the principle of the bill, which is to increase the capital from $200 million to $400 million and also to carry out certain administrative amendments. I find a little difficulty in following the argument of the hon. member at this stage. He may have a point that is quite related at a later stage, but if he is only using this as an illustration of his argument on the principle under discussion then he may continue. On the other hand if his argument is going to be along the lines he is suggesting, perhaps he could defer it.

I was just bringing it up in so far as it referred to small exporters, and I know that some of them, in written legal opinion, have been told that they did not qualify under the act in that they were not regularly employed as exporters. I am willing to defer that question to a later time when this bill is under consideration in committee. However, Mr. Speaker, I would say that this act has been a good one. It was introduced into this house in 1944 and helped
to make Canada the third trading nation in the world. I think we were the first nation, on a per capita basis, in this respect.
I think it is all the more important, therefore, to bring this measure forward now in order to do everything we can to help our exporters, because in this country one in every five jobs depends upon our export trade. It is all the more important to do this at the present time because our position in world trade has fallen from third to eighth or ninth place.
I should like to ask the minister, in regard to exports to Cuba, whether any use has been made of this act by anybody. The minister explained the export of wheat to China very satisfactorily yesterday. I should also like to know, when the minister replies, whether or not the National Steamships' ships sold to Cuba were in any way sold under this act; also, whether we have received any payment in respect of those ships, and who will be assuming the loss, if any has to be assumed.

Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Chown in the chair.

Mr. Chairman, in connection with clause 2 the important point, of course, is the change from $200 million to $400 million. I think this is an appropriate time for us to have a statement from the minister in respect to the priorities of our exports. In the discussion thus far there has been a great deal of attention given to the export of grains and raw materials of various kinds. I would have thought that in a measure of this kind we should first of all endeavour to assist the export of Canadian products abroad which contain as high a content of Canadian labour as possible. I think my hon. friend from Okanagan Boundary made that statement, and I saw him some time ago applaud wildly when the statement was made that the record to date was good. I say to him that as far as his own area is concerned, rather than supporting the sale abroad of Okanagan apples- they require no credit, of course; they are of such high quality-he should be much more interested in the sale of mechanical giraffes. My hon. friend from that area has a firm that not only invented a machine but has sold it, I think, widely around the world, which carries men up to the tops of poles, and so on, to put on wires. I think they are in Ontario as well.
I am asking the minister now whether any attention is given to selectivity so far as the

Export Credits Insurance Act extension of credit is concerned, so that we can as far as possible sell those products which are invented in Canada and are new to the countries to which we sell them; in other words, give the corporation in Canada a leg up in that market in connection with articles that are so good that thereafter the country will demand them and find the money to pay for them.
It seems to me this should be the first interest of this corporation, rather than the unloading of vast surpluses of raw materials.
I regret very much that in the experience we have had thus far the great proportion of the credit extended seems to have been for the unloading of surplus materials which we could not otherwise sell. I am not disparaging the sale of wheat, but I know something about farming and I wish to tell hon. members that I saw in the area of the Peace river country not very long ago one farmer with a considerable amount of machinery, one man, who this year swept the crop off 755 acres. This is not maintaining a great number of Canadian homes.
If we wish to take care of the unemployment situation in this country we have to emphasize and advance quickly those goods which employ an increasing amount of Canadian labour in their manufacture.

Mr. Chairman, I was very interested in the remarks of the hon. member from Vancouver South, but I would point out to him that the assistance of credit from this corporation is available to everyone in the export business who solicits help. Speaking of priority, I should like to ask the minister this question. Under section 21(a) of this act, where it is necessary for the governor in council to extend long term credits, is there anything new in regard to the proposed sale of $30 million worth of railway cars of high Canadian labour content which are manufactured in Hamilton? Also, has the corporation given any consideration or discussed with National Steel Car of Hamilton their negotiations with the government of Argentina, South America, so as to ascertain whether it will be feasible to extend long term credit to that government? I understand National Steel Car of Hamilton is negotiating in this respect.
I think this is a prime indication that our government is not only looking after the interests of the wheat farmer and the agricultural part of the community, but has been actively engaged in helping manufacturers of heavy equipment to try and get into the markets of the world with the assistance of long term credit.
I would point out that section 21(a) is the only part of the act under which the governor

in council is required to give authorization. The rest of the act may be acted upon by the corporation without this authorization.

Mr. Chairman, if I can keep current with these questions, I should like to do as I did at the resolution stage and answer first the question of the hon. member for Vancouver South. The hon. member expressed concern that the facilities of the corporation under this act are used mostly to dispose of surplus commodities, as he rather disparagingly refers to them.
Not disparagingly.

He was rather downgrading them, as I understood it. I should like to ask him, and any hon. members of the official opposition, to stand up and say if they are against the assistance which this government has given to the sale of wheat to many countries of the world. I have heard them make, for a long time now, and it makes me a little annoyed to keep hearing them over and over again, as many snide cracks and disparaging remarks, it seems, as they possibly can against our assisting wheat farmers to get rid of their wheat, for which we are paid. We are not giving away any of our wheat surpluses.
That was Social Credit.

We are being paid for them, and the arrangement is greatly beneficial to the farmers of Canada. I should like to ask hon. members on the other side to tell us once and for all whether they are in favour of assistance to our wheat sales or whether they are not. If they are not, let them get on their feet and say so.

Because my name has been brought into this argument by the minister I think I might say a word or two. He said I had been downgrading farmers and speaking in a snide voice. I did none of those things, as hon. members well know. I did suggest that we should have priorities and that priority should be given to the expansion of export of those products which have a high labour content. I want to tell the minister that I personally am in favour of the sale of all Canadian commodities abroad, including wheat, but let us have an insistence upon those things which employ most Canadian families and keep most Canadians at work.

I am glad the hon. member brought that up because the operation of section 21(l)(a), which this government brought into operation to provide a service to exporters and business people in this country of ours, does precisely that. It was a service for which they had asked the government of

the party to which the hon. member belongs for many years without any results whatever. They asked the government for it in those days and were turned down. Finally, we produced a long term financial arrangement, and if the hon. member would just read this act instead of just talking about it, he could see what the requirements are. The basic requirement in section 21(l)(a) with regard to assistance for long term financing is that there must be at least an 80 per cent content of Canadian parts or products.
I should like to remind the hon. member again that in the operation of this section this government is providing the businessmen and exporters of this country with a service equal to that provided by any government in the world, if not better. That is something which the former government steadfastly refused to do, and the result of this neglect was to handicap the exporters, manufacturers and shippers of this country. It was a case of refusing to meet their legitimate demands. By taking the action we have, assistance has been given to Canadian producers of capital goods-goods with a high labour content- in selling over $50 million worth of their products.
At the present time negotiations are actively being conducted with regard to a further $75 million worth of such products, and we hope that sales will be made. Such sales never could have been made but for the policy being followed by the present government. I want the hon. member to know that since it began operating in 1944 significant results have been obtained in just those categories to which he made reference. I will mention three different commodities, all of which have a large labour content. This corporation has insured $49,525,000 worth of flour; it has insured $138,312,000 worth of farm machinery; it has insured $116,995,000 worth of steel. I mention only three products, but the list is a very long one indeed. I say to the hon. member for Vancouver South and to other hon. members opposite that this corporation exists for the sole purpose of providing insurance and long term financing covering every type of product. As I said in my opening remarks it covers every type of commodity and every type of producer in all parts of Canada.
Again I ask members of this house to let their constituents know that this service is available to them. We hope they will come to us and use the services of this corporation. The doors of this corporation are always open, as are the doors of the ministers of this government. We exist for the sole purpose of helping Canadian producers help themselves to increase sales of all Canadian commodities
Export Credits Insurance Act in all parts of the world. I assure the hon. member that we are trying to sell every type of commodity in every way we can every day of the week, and I am told by businessmen of this country that the activities of this government compared with those of the government which preceded it are as night is to day-they are the night, and we are the day.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member for Rose-dale did rise earlier, as a matter of fact, but I did not see him. I apologize for not having done so, because he had hoped to speak on clause 1. I hope the committee will allow him the latitude he deserves because he did not have that opportunity.

Thank you very much. I wish to address a question to the minister with regard to the term "capital surplus" which occurs in the clause and also with regard to the financial position of the corporation. What function does the capital surplus perform? In a public commercial corporation I can see it might have some relevance but in this case I would suggest that the entire holding be capitalized as subscribed capital and the category of capital surplus thereby eliminated. There would therefore be no necessity for such words to be used in clause 1 and they could be deleted.
I am sorry. It may be the acoustics or in the way the hon. member is speaking, but what he is saying is not clear to me. Perhaps he would repeat what he has said.

What function does capital surplus represent on the balance sheet of this corporation? I am suggesting to the minister that the entire holding should be represented by the subscribed capital of $10 million. The necessity for carrying a capital surplus account and for introducing the two words in clause 1 might therefore be eliminated. It may be there is some historical or statutory reason for this surplus and I would appreciate the minister's advice on this point.

I am advised that the corporation was set up in 1944 in this way for the following reason: the $5 million of capital surplus was there so that if there were any losses in the first few years the actual capital of the corporation would remain intact.
While I am on my feet, I should like to answer the question raised by the hon. member for Hamilton South regarding Argentine box cars. The history of this is that three Canadian box car companies were negotiating with the Argentine railway companies for the sale of box cars valued at some $35 million. There was also a prospect of selling

Export Credits Insurance Act another $25 million worth of Canadian products, which have a very high labour content, and we were doing our best to help these companies under section 21(l)(a). During the negotiations there was a change in the Argentine government and the decision to place orders was deferred. As far as we know at this time, the possibility of Argentina placing orders in Canada for box cars still exists. I was talking to one of the gentlemen concerned just yesterday about it. I know that the negotiations are still active. I can assure the hon. member for Hamilton South, who has been very active in this and shown great interest, and also the hon. member for Pictou, who has shown a tremendous interest along with the hon. member for Hamilton South, and who has seen me many times on a number of occasions, that the corporation and the government are continuing to extend every effort to help in every way they can these three Canadian companies who are trying so hard to land this very important order for box cars which will be of great benefit to the economy as a whole and to employment in general in these three important areas.

Mr. Chairman, I do not want to start the minister off on another flaming peroration, although he can start off anyway he likes if it would help us, but I would ask him to tell me where we find in the act reference to the 80 per cent labour content?
You cannot; it is not in it.
It is not written into the act.
Oh, oh.

You are talking about a section of the act that you never even bothered using. As another example of the constructive approach of this government to problems of this kind, to make sure that a high Canadian content should be contained in products for which we provide this export financing, it was the decision and the practice of this government that we would not grant this long term financing under section 21(a) to projects which did not contain 80 per cent content.

Mr. Chairman, the minister, under the guise of discussing the matter before the committee, has gone into a mass of detail which does much to damage the administration of the act. One of the problems facing exporters and producers in this country at this time is the feeling of uncertainty in the absence of government policies. When we have before the house an amending bill in respect of an act which has worked rather well since its inception in 1944, an amendment on specific points of the act in order to bring it up to date so that it will meet the
[Mr. Hees.l
conditions of 1962 and 1963, instead of making careful statements of policy of the government which could be relied on by industry, we get the inaccurate and confusing loud speeches of the minister, such as the last three he has just made to the committee tonight.
First of all, I want to point out some of the inaccuracies, and I do this for the benefit of his understudy from Oxford, who does not seem to be too familiar with the effect of the operation of the act on the economy of this country, or its implication as evidenced by his little travelogue a few days ago when this measure was at the resolution stage.
The first inaccuracy has to do with his rather windy question, after some orations about the wheat sales in western CanaSa. Since those wheat sales were first announced, two things have become abundantly clear. One is that the government would not give the proper information to the House of Commons. That is supported by the record of the last parliament; and if any hon. member requires further elucidation, he can get it from Hansard of the last parliament.
The other matter which is abundantly clear is that all members of the House of Commons concurred in and approved of the sale of the wheat to China, but some hon. members asked about the irregularity of taking taxpayers money and using it without the approval of the House of Commons for the purpose of granting credit to communist China. That was the point of issue in that transaction, and that is the point that was slurred over by the minister tonight when he asked hon. members sitting opposite the government if they approved those sales. If they had said yes, then he would have come out and said that they approved of this irregularity in guaranteeing the $100 million, and of using public funds improperly instead of using them under the two legal means available to the government in getting that credit. Indeed, at the resolution stage on Friday he indicated that this measure now before us could and would be used to finance this kind of sale, and he indicated the sales to other communist countries which had been dealt with under this act. They are some of the inaccuracies so far.
Then another inaccuracy was in talking about the 80 per cent content requirement. That is not in the legislation. That is something which the government has imported of its own accord into its administration of the act. It is interesting that he has chosen to do it that way rather than to put it in the act. I would suggest to hon. members opposite that if the government is importing conditions of this kind, although I think this one

is satisfactory, when will there be a condition imported that will not be satisfactory?
I suggest that the real question is involved in this clause of the bill and the one following, and that is that we are providing the governor in council with $300 million of authority, to be spent on different competing contractors in this country, which is to be allocated on the say-so of the cabinet to one particular contractor or exporter as against another. There is a very grave danger there. While desirable to over-all trade, under a careless or irresponsible government-and we have heard the speech of the minister at Ghana in the trade field about applying patronage methods-this clause can be very sinister. I think it would better serve the exporters of this country if he would speak carefully and outline what the government's policy is with respect to its administration of this very large sum of money being granted by this house for the benefit of our exporters in order to enable them to compete in export markets. That is the kind of statement we want from the minister.
Then there are other remarks which the minister made about the use of the act and the use the former government made of it; and he went on to say that there was the difference of night and day between the two governments in the whole field of trade. That, Mr. Chairman, is perfectly correct; there is all the difference between night and day. Under the former government there was prosperity in the country. What the exporters required in those days, as anybody who reads the legislation and follows it in relation to the times, and who reads the debates when it was passed, well knows, was insurance because of the currency difficulties of foreign countries. It was not a matter of Canadian exporters not being able to compete in those days with foreign countries; it was a matter of insuring the risk in collecting the money from foreign countries. Indeed, part II of the act still before us dealt with another situation where governments in the war devastated countries were so disorganized that they could not provide the currency because of their exchange difficulties. That is the kind of criterion which had to be the test of legislation in those days.
The minister talks now about the former government's not passing the amending clause to this act. That was not required until the re-establishment of industry in west Germany, Great Britain, Italy and those other countries when they became competitors with our manufacturers and exporters. That was the reason section 21(a) became so necessary and so desirable. But that section 21(a) was not required when those countries had their industries devastated and were not in a position to supply world demands.
Export Credits Insurance Act
Hence when the minister makes loose and careless statements about the former government in relation to this legislation, he shows a lack of understanding of the problems affecting industry. That is the kind of thing that destroys confidence in the country and indeed contributes to the economic difficulties in which this country finds itself. While the minister's excursions into some of his barnstorming political talks may be interesting and amusing to members of the committee, perhaps he could arrange another forum for them-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Don't be bitter.

-and could here bring before hon. members matters which are relevant to the bill before us and which would do something to assist production in this country and the exporters of this country. Indeed, when he was asked a question having to do with assisting exporters who would provide a large amount of employment in this country, I would have thought he would have been very careful to deal responsibly with the question, as the problem of lack of employment for people in this country must surely weigh heavily on the minds of all hon. members on all sides of this chamber.

I was most interested to hear the hon. member for Ottawa West harking back to what he would consider the good old days, the 22 years when patronage really ran rampant. From listening to him talk, you would think we were doing the kind of things that happened when they were in power, when deals were made with specific firms that were friendly and so on. That is something that does not happen any more.
That was when the act was born.

At the outset, Mr. Chairman,
inasmuch as this is the first opportunity I have had to say anything in committee, I should like to extend to you on behalf of the members of this party our congratulations on your attaining the office you now hold. We look forward to working with you intimately on all matters over which you will be presiding. Now that this family squabble between
[Mr. Hees.l

the Liberals and the Tories has perhaps reached some sort of end, maybe we can get back to the meat of the subject before us.
First, I should like to say that this selfadoration which the minister heaped all over himself reminds me that perhaps his position is that of acting prime minister today. That is a position to which I am sure he is not objecting. However, it really is a bit sad to hear the minister gloat so openly and so profusely about a particular change that was made in the act in 1960-61, namely section 21(a). He lauded this as one of the most progressive steps that he and his government had made in the field of assisting our exporters in this country.
I just contrast that statement made by the minister with what he had to say on October 12 when this matter was at the resolution stage. The minister, in dealing with section 21(a) about which he is now gloating, admitted that it came into effect by default and that really he or his government had nothing to do with it; that it was not a question of any great desire on the part of the minister to do something proper and correct for our exporters and for the economy of this nation but it was something that arose by default. What does the minister say about it? As found at page 474 of Hansard, when dealing with these great free enterprisers of whom he is so greatly enamoured, he states as follows:
Well, Mr. Chairman, the operation which the Export Credits Insurance Corporation carries out under section 21(a)-
That is the one about which he was gloating a moment ago as being a mark of leadership on his part or on the part of the government.
-was literally forced upon it by the unwillingness of Canadian banks to perform this function for our exporters.
Private enterprise failed. Because private enterprise, so-called, failed, the minister then gloats about it and lauds this as one of the principal things that has been done by his government and condemns the party opposite, which is now the official opposition, for having failed to accomplish something like this in the 22 years in which they were in office. In essence, so far as I am concerned, the Liberals would have done precisely the same thing if they were forced into it, not by way of leadership, design, intimate concern for the exporters of this country, or concern for the undeveloped nations, the one element in the world with which we should be concerning ourselves; no, Mr. Speaker, by default and by default only. I will disregard for the moment these comments on the side that impinge upon my ear. I would gladly deal with them if those making them would do so

in a loud enough voice so that other hon. members could hear them and so that they would get on the record. Let them do it in the proper fashion.
In the clause with which we are now dealing we are concerned and should be concerned with what this parliament can do with respect to assistance to underdeveloped countries. These are the people in the world with whom we are going to have to concern ourselves if we have any concern about world peace at all. These are the countries that are emerging economically, socially and politically. These are countries which are practically stone broke. These are countries to whom we have to give some assistance. These are countries which we have to help along the economic road. These are countries that cannot now afford to buy the things they would like to buy and we as a nation are being niggardly about it. We are complaining about the fact that we are exporting raw materials when we have surpluses of them everywhere and we do nothing worth while except when forced into the position of acting when our great banking and financial institutions fail to act.
All the minister has to do is to read his own words from pages 474 and 475 of Hansard for October 12. Not only should he read them but let them have some meaning for him. If these words really do mean something to you, Mr. Minister, and to your government then you will take some steps to amend this particular section to provide the same things as were provided under section 23 of the act as it existed in 1952 and as was the case prior to 1948. You will take steps to ensure that the governor in council will lend money to other countries that cannot afford to buy our products and thus help them to build up their economies so that their income will be sufficiently large for them to be able to pay for these things eventually.
We have to extend assistance to them and we are not going to assist them and assist our exporters to any marked degree so long as the government persists in carrying on the same sort of verbal fencing that the Liberals did for the 22 years they were in office. Unfortunately that is all you are doing, just gloating about something that you came upon by accident and indicating that this is the sole effort you are putting forward so far as this country is concerned. Again we have these inane gentlemen over here interjecting. I used to be able to call them the gentlemen opposite. I still can in one sense, but while the line of demarcation between us is very thin it is a gulf that will never be bridged so far as I am concerned because this government-I do not know whether my friend
Export Credits Insurance Act realizes it-is only concerned with buttressing the faltering free enterprise system at every opportunity.
What would you suggest?
My friend says, "What would I suggest". I just suggested something.
All I have heard you do is use the word "gloat" about forty times.

You remind me of my aunt's parrot. All you are concerned about is asking questions. You are not concerned about getting an answer. I will tell my hon. friend the answer if he will listen. I do not know if it will do him any good to listen but I will tell him anyway. I have already told him quite distinctly that we should amend the act to provide precisely what was provided in what was section 23, which the minister's department removed in the consolidation, and make arrangements so that the government of Canada can, and I quote, "make a loan to the government or any agency of the government of any such other country to enable such government or such agency or any person ordinarily resident in such other country to pay the cost of Canadian-produced goods purchased from an exporter or the cost of Canadian services". That is one item.
Do you want us to go against the Speaker's ruling?

Once again, Mr. Chairman, I appeal to you to protect me against these inanities. As I indicated earlier, the hon. member is like my aunt's parrot. He is not interested in an answer but merely wants to repeat the question.
A pretty smart parrot.

I have given an answer, not in my own words but in the words of the section of the Export Credits Insurance Act as found in chapter 105 of the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1952, an answer which was the answer of Canada prior to January 1, 1948, after which time the section no longer had validity. If we had had a Liberal government with any sense about these things they would have re-enacted the section or brought it into force again so that we could have used it. There is one of the answers, one of the things that we suggest.
My friend may interpret the Speaker's ruling differently from me, but I should like very much to have the minister explain to us, in simple, uncomplicated terms so that his own followers can understand, what the government is going to do about this very important question raised initially by my friend from Danforth and mentioned by other hon. members. That important question is,
560	HOUSE OF
Export Credits Insurance Act what can this country, Canada, what can this parliament, a group of minorities, do by co-operation to ensure the highest possible degree of export of Canadian made goods and thus improve our own economic structure and also assist other countries in the world community to participate in economic development?

Mr. Chairman, I am very glad to answer that question in the few minutes left this evening. What the hon. member and his colleague from Danforth have asked is that we should provide long term loans to developing countries. This is, as I pointed out earlier, one of the purposes of section 21(a) as it operates at the present time and as it will operate more efficiently when the present bill is passed. I might say that section 21(a) already provides no less than $300 million for this exact purpose. Already contracts under section 21(a) amounting to more than $50 million have been signed and commitments have been given for additional business totalling $75 million, all in developing countries.
As an example of the type of loans being made under section 21(a), I can mention the $25 million credit extended by Canada to India and the $15 million credit to Pakistan. In addition to this amount of aid to developing countries the government assists such countries by Colombo plan aid amounting to $50 million a year, aid to Africa amounting to $10.5 million, aid to the West Indies amounting to $10 million, technical assistance aid to French language commonwealth countries and, lastly, our participation in the international bank for reconstruction and development and its associated organs, one of which is the international development association. The international development association was established to make so-called soft loans, somewhere between a loan and a gift, to the developing countries, and Canada's contribution in this respect is $38 million.
I think that gives a pretty good idea of what this government is doing to help the developing countries about which the hon. member has just spoken. I think all hon. members will agree that Canada today is doing her share in helping these very worthy developing countries to develop and help themselves.
Clause 2 agreed to.

On clause 3-Power to lend or guarantee, etc.
Progress reported.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: May I ask if there is any change in the order of business as announced on Friday and, if there is, what will be the order of business for tomorrow?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we shall carry on with this bill, No. C-63, as the first item tomorrow. We shall then deal with the resolution in the name of the Minister of Agriculture which is No. 17 on today's order paper, dealing with the Farm Credit Act. The third item will be second reading of Bill No. C-3, an act to amend the Food and Drugs Act.
I doubt very much if the house will get further than that tomorrow but, if it does, there are some items on the order paper which would not consume too much time and might be fitted in. If there is a short period available I would suggest that hon. members be ready to deal with item No. 9 on today's order paper, second reading of Bill C-58, an act to amend the Carriage by Air Act, in the name of the Minister of Transport; No. 10 on today's order paper, also in the name of the Minister of Transport, respecting public harbours, and if the house moves very quickly we might even take No. 23 on today's order paper, also in the name of the Minister of Transport and dealing with the Aeronautics Act.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: May I ask the house leader what has become of the resolution which he called in the third place on Friday, having to do with redistribution?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: It is still on the order paper, Mr. Speaker. The reason I have not called it is simply because we did not move as quickly today as we anticipated. I thought we would have finished the bill dealing with the Export Credits Insurance Corporation and the resolution on the Farm Credit Act; but obviously we cannot complete them and the food and drugs measure plus the electoral boundaries resolution tomorrow.
It being three minutes after ten o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
